change.title: docs: plan join tabs, group sharing and device identity
change.body:
Docs only. No code changes. Plans the next round of joining, sharing and identity work. It also writes down the later reliability design so earlier changes don't block it.

**PRD IDs:** C2 (withdrawn), C3, C15, C16, F10–F18, N4, S2, S3, S18–S20, R1–R5, OQ9, OQ10 · **Threat IDs:** T-S6, T-S7, T-S8, T-T5, T-R1, T-I12, T-D10, MUC9, MUC10

## What changes
- **Joining screens (PRD UC2, C15, C16):** orbs are withdrawn (C2). Screens join by tapping join tabs on facing edges or with a mini-map where each person moves only their own tile and the other device must accept. Both have Undo or "No".
- **Sharing in a group (F11–F15, UC9):** joined screens receive by themselves up to 20 MB, "Share with everyone" with a tray, "Save all" and later receipts and catch-up for late arrivals.
- **Dragging (F16–F18):** a print can't get stuck at a screen's edge or on a shared edge, click to pick up and drop on laptops and drags stay clear of the phone's own gestures.
- **Identity (S2, S18–S20):** a reload is the same device coming back, names are unique per room by a name key (case, full-width letters, accents, invisible characters and mixed scripts), remembered devices are off by default and each device has a colour and icon from its key. The four words (S3) become an optional "Check this device" step.
- **Later (PRD 7.6, ARCHITECTURE 13):** piece hashes, any holder sends any piece, spreading through the room, chaos tests and a dashboard, repair pieces.
- **Threat model and test plan:** new threats, misuse cases MUC9 and MUC10 plus a test row for every new requirement.

## Notes
- S2 follows #24's design: the device id is the hash of its public key. Only room messages and passed-on data get an extra ECDSA signature.
- Keys can't go in `sessionStorage` (it only stores text), so S18 keeps a tab id there and the keys in IndexedDB.
- `AGENTS.md` still says "push orbs". It changes with the code when C15 ships, not in this PR.
- ARCHITECTURE 13 lists two bugs in today's code: missing pieces are only asked from the first sender. Pieces already received are thrown away when a link falls back to the relay. They get their own ticket.
- Tickets for these requirements are filed after this merges.

+| **Lives** | Today in memory only: reloading makes new keys. Planned (S18): every device's keys are stored in IndexedDB as non-exportable keys for the tab's lifetime, so a reload keeps them (see Identity). They are deleted when the tab closes, at the latest at the next start-up. Leave deletes them too (S13). The host's keys are kept until the room expires (S11), so the fingerprint in shared links keeps matching. Keys outlive the tab only with "Remember this device" (S20) |
+| **Accepted** | The first key from each device. Later keys are ignored. Verifying keys with four words is planned (S3), as an optional "Check this device" step |
+| **Tied to the id (planned, S2, #24)** | A device's id is the first 128 bits of the SHA-256 of its two public keys (encryption then signing, each in raw form), in base64url. Both keys are announced together. Keys that don't hash to their id are dropped, so nobody can claim another device's id or attach their own signing key to it. No signed message is accepted until its sender's keys have been checked against its id |
+| **Signing (planned, S2)** | A second key pair, ECDSA P-256, made at the same time and also non-exportable. Its public key is announced in presence. Room messages (which every device sees, so no pair key covers them) and anything passed on for someone else (piece hashes, R1) are signed with it. Every device checks the signature and drops anything that doesn't match |
+
+### 6.1 Identity (planned: S2, S18, S19, S20)
+There are no accounts. A device is known by what it holds, not by who the person is.
+
+| Part | Where it comes from | How long it lasts |
+|---|---|---|
+| Device id | Today random. Planned: the hash of both public keys (S2, #24), so it lasts as long as the keys | The tab's lifetime (S18) |
+| Name | Typed by the person. Checked by `validName`, compared by its name key (S19) | The tab's lifetime |
+| Encryption and signing keys | Made in the browser. The private keys can't be exported | The tab's lifetime. Longer only if the person turns on "Remember this device" (S20) |
+| Colour and three emoji | Picked from the id: one of 12 colours and three emoji from a list of 128, about 2²⁵ looks. A visual aid only: a key can be made over and over until its look matches someone's, so nothing relies on it | As long as the keys |
+
+**Surviving a reload (S18).** `sessionStorage` holds a random tab id, which survives a reload and is cleared when the tab closes. Keys can't go in `sessionStorage` (it only stores text), so they are kept in IndexedDB as non-exportable `CryptoKey` objects under that tab id. Each tab holds a Web Lock named after its tab id for as long as it is open (`navigator.locks.request(tabId, …)`). On load, a tab with a stored tab id asks for that lock with `ifAvailable: true`. If it gets it, it is the same tab after a reload and reuses its id, name and keys. "Duplicate tab" copies `sessionStorage`, so a duplicate has the same tab id. The original still holds the lock: the duplicate can't get it, so it makes a new tab id and starts as a new device. On every start-up the site also tries the lock of each other stored tab id. A free lock means that tab has closed, so its keys are deleted. Received files and pieces are never stored, only kept in memory (S13).
+
+**Names (S19).** The name key, used only for comparing:
+```js
+// accents come off Latin, Greek and Cyrillic letters only: Indic vowel signs are marks too and must stay
+const nameKey = (s) => s.normalize('NFKC').normalize('NFD')
+  .replace(/([\p{Script=Latin}\p{Script=Greek}\p{Script=Cyrillic}])\p{M}+/gu, '$1').normalize('NFC')
+  .toUpperCase().toLowerCase().trim().replace(/\s+/g, ' ');
+```
+`toUpperCase().toLowerCase()` also folds `ß` to `ss`. `toLocaleLowerCase()` isn't used, because Turkish `İ` and `ı` change with the locale. `validName` refuses:
+- control characters, private-use and unassigned code points plus invisible format characters: zero-width space, word joiner, `U+FEFF` and every text-direction control (`U+200E`, `U+200F`, `U+061C`, `U+202A`–`U+202E`, `U+2066`–`U+2069`). The zero-width joiner and non-joiner are allowed only between two letters or two emoji, because emoji such as 👩‍👩‍👧 and scripts such as Persian and Devanagari need them;
+- script mixes that UTS #39's "Highly Restrictive" level doesn't allow. Each character's `Script_Extensions` must fit one script or one of Latin + Han + Hiragana + Katakana (Japanese), Latin + Han + Bopomofo or Latin + Han + Hangul (Korean). Common and Inherited characters (digits, punctuation, emoji) fit with any. So `Ѕam` (Cyrillic Ѕ with Latin) is refused and `山田さくら` is allowed;
+- names longer than 24 characters as seen on screen (counted with `Intl.Segmenter`).
+
+Two kinds of look-alike can't all be caught: look-alikes inside one script ("5am", "rn" for "m") and a name written entirely in another script that happens to look the same (Cyrillic `сор` beside Latin `cop`). Neither can the colour and emoji, which only help honest people tell devices apart. "New device" (S20) and the four words (S3) are what catch a deliberate look-alike.
+
+**Remembered devices (S20).** Off by default and only ever the person's own choice. When turned on, the device's keys are kept in IndexedDB until "Forget". Its presence then says `remember: true`. Other devices store the public keys and name only of devices whose presence says `remember: true`, also in IndexedDB. Nobody stores a device that didn't opt in. When a device turns it off or taps Forget, its presence says `remember: false` and devices that see that delete what they stored for it. A device whose key is known shows "seen before". A known name on a key that isn't known shows "new device". Nothing about this is sent to the server.

The vendored exifr library can read metadata but not remove it | High | Medium | S6 covers JPEG first (`web/strip.js`, which copies the image segments it keeps and drops the rest). Every other file (HEIC, PNG, WebP, video) is sent with a "details not removed" warning. S17 covers the other formats later. Check whether the iPhone file picker already converts HEIC to JPEG |
+
+## 13. Later: spreading pieces through the room (R1–R5)
+Not built. Today a file comes from one holder at a time and every pair of devices can link directly. This is the design the later requirements point at, so changes before then don't block it.
+
+**Two networks, as now.** The room server is a star: presence, the clock, joins and introductions. The devices form a mesh for content. A private send ("Send to…") always uses one direct link between the two devices or the sealed relay. It never travels through a third device. Only shared-with-everyone and joined-group files spread.
+
+**Where data gets lost today and what handles it**
+| Layer | Loses data? | Handled by |
+|---|---|---|
+| One WebRTC link | Packets drop. Data channels are reliable and ordered: SCTP resends only the missing parts (selective acknowledgements) | The browser |
+| The relay | Yes. Supabase broadcasts have no acknowledgement and can be dropped under load | `need`: the receiver lists the missing pieces every 1.5 s and only those are sent again |
+| A holder going away | Yes: a phone locks, leaves or goes slow | Today: the transfer asks the same device again and gives up after a minute (C12). Later: R2 |
+
+**Gaps in today's code that R2 closes:** `need` always goes to the device the transfer started with, even when other holders are listed. Pieces are only accepted from that one device. A change of piece size (direct to relay) throws away the pieces already received. A bad piece is only found by the whole-file SHA-256 at the end, so the whole file is fetched again and the sender can't be told apart. "I have it" claims aren't checked. The whole file is held in memory.
+
+**Each piece has a state**
+```mermaid
+stateDiagram-v2
+  [*] --> Missing
+  Missing --> Requested: ask a holder (rarest first)
+  Requested --> Checking: arrives
+  Requested --> Missing: timeout or the holder left
+  Checking --> Have: piece hash matches (R1)
+  Checking --> Missing: hash wrong, sender gets a strike
+  Have --> [*]
+```
+
+**How it spreads (R3).** Each device links to a few neighbours (about 4–6: its joined screens plus a few others), so links grow with the number of devices instead of its square. Devices tell their neighbours which pieces they hold. Rarest pieces are asked for first. Each device serves only a few others at once. The sender hands different pieces to different neighbours first. Near the end, the last pieces are asked from several holders and the first to arrive wins, so one slow phone can't hold up the finish (Rule 3). Requests in flight are capped per neighbour and every request has a timeout.
+
+**Repair pieces (R5).** Only if R4 shows the relay losing a lot. Reed–Solomon adds a fixed number of repair pieces. Fountain codes (RaptorQ, for example) can make any number, so different devices can send different repair pieces without coordinating. Either costs encoding work on phones.
+
+**Why not a library.** WebTorrent does this in the browser over WebRTC. It brings its own wire protocol and public trackers, which don't fit the Deaf Relay rule. It is also a large dependency to review. A small version built on the existing messages and checks fits better.
